hits.text: Our Amazon research obtained 18 product detail records across 15 brands. The most useful finding is not which mushroom is “hottest,” but how differently products describe their materials and quantities. The sample includes fruiting-body extracts, mycelium with fermented substrate, single-mushroom capsules, coffee with collagen, and gummies containing other botanical ingredients.

Blended capsules show a similar contrast. [FreshCap Ultimate](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07NY3WR4L) lists six mushrooms and uses the blend-level phrase “100% whole fruiting body mushrooms.” [Host Defense MyCommunity](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B002WJ1BZK) lists 17 species and describes mycelium grown on organic brown rice, referring to both mycelium and fermented rice substrate. Species count does not establish composition or individual ingredient doses.[14][15]

A useful comparison therefore separates species, tissue source, fermented substrate, extraction form and quantity per serving. These fields are not a ranking of efficacy or material quality. In particular, a blend-level fruiting-body statement does not establish the anatomical material used for every ingredient, including chaga.

Liquids need their own units as well. [Host Defense reishi liquid](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0062RC9ZO) supplies dropper instructions and refers to mycelium and fermented rice substrate. Dropper frequency alone does not establish extract mass in milligrams.[8]

title: "Choosing Carob Powder for Cocoa Replacement: Roast Level, Recipe Basis and Cake Texture"
description: "Compare carob roast positioning, cake recipe bases and texture evidence before replacing cocoa; distinguish pulp powder from locust bean gum."
tags: ["Carob", "Cocoa", "Baking"]

Start with the cocoa flavor you want to retain. Worldwide Botanicals gives its two retail powders different roles: the [medium roast](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07JX6YCKR) is positioned for regular cocoa and milk-chocolate-style recipes, while the [dark roast](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0F67QBGL3) is positioned for dark cocoa and dark-chocolate-style recipes. These are the seller's suggested uses, not results of an equivalence test.[6][7]

That distinction is more useful than looking for a generic “cocoa substitute.” It helps define the first sample comparison. Deciding how much to use, whether to change wheat flour and whether the cake will become denser still requires formulation evidence. Two baking studies illustrate the central issue: **similar acceptance does not mean identical flavor, and a published percentage is not necessarily a cocoa replacement rate.**[3][4]
<table class="carob-table">

Product and ASINWorldwide Botanicals medium roast, B07JX6YCKRHow the listing positions itUses “regular cocoa” and recipes calling for milk chocolate as reference points.[6]Question for a sample trialDo sweetness, cocoa taste and baked aroma work together in the target cake?

Product and ASINWorldwide Botanicals dark roast, B0F67QBGL3How the listing positions itUses “dark cocoa” and recipes calling for dark chocolate as reference points.[7]Question for a sample trialDoes the baked product achieve the intended color and flavor, rather than merely starting with a darker powder?

Product and ASINThe Australian Carob Co., B01D2975KSHow the listing positions itTitled “Raw,” under The Australian Carob Co.; product bullets are absent from the detail sample.[8]Question for a sample trialIf the aim is a deliberately carob-flavored product, is this worth testing alongside roasted candidates?

The medium and dark products belong to the same brand, making them useful examples of how a seller segments its range by target flavor. The Raw product is not that brand's third roast level. A cross-brand comparison can also introduce differences in raw material and processing, so any observed difference cannot automatically be attributed to roasting alone.[6][7][8] The Raw detail capture also labels the item type “Video Game,” inconsistent with its title. We therefore use only its title and brand as positioning evidence, not as confirmation of processing temperature, nutrition or quality.[8]

A milk-chocolate-style use case does not establish that a powder can replace the milk chocolate in a recipe gram for gram. Nor do these listings define “dark cocoa” as a specified alkalization level or pH.[6][7] A useful sample request should therefore state whether the existing ingredient is cocoa powder or chocolate, and which flavor attributes must be retained—not simply request medium or dark roast.

These pages offer positioning, not a controlled performance comparison. We do not adopt their health, low-calorie, cost-saving or “perfect replacement” claims, or infer sales from search positions and review counts. Roast choices also exist in industrial supply: [Nordmann's introduction to Carob Ingredients](https://www.nordmann.global/en/news-events/news/exquisite-carob-products-from-morocco) lists light, medium and dark roasted pulp powders for baked goods and cocoa drinks, but provides no same-recipe comparison across those roasts.[2]
## “30% carob” does not mean replacing 30% of the cocoa
A 2020 Madeira-type cake study used commercial roasted flour from Creta Carob, not the three retail samples above. Its 100% flour basis was the combined 75 g of wheat flour, cocoa and carob flour.[3]
<table class="carob-table">

<thead><tr><th scope="col">Study treatment</th><th scope="col">Wheat flour</th><th scope="col">Cocoa powder</th><th scope="col">Carob pulp flour</th><th scope="col">Carob share of the listed 300 g ingredient total, calculated here</th></tr></thead><tbody>
Study treatmentControlWheat flour60 gCocoa powder15 gCarob pulp flour0Carob share of the listed 300 g ingredient total, calculated here0
Study treatment10Wheat flour67.5 gCocoa powder0Carob pulp flour7.5 gCarob share of the listed 300 g ingredient total, calculated here2.5%
Study treatment30Wheat flour52.5 gCocoa powder0Carob pulp flour22.5 gCarob share of the listed 300 g ingredient total, calculated here7.5%
Study treatment50Wheat flour37.5 gCocoa powder0Carob pulp flour37.5 gCarob share of the listed 300 g ingredient total, calculated here12.5%
Study treatment70Wheat flour22.5 gCocoa powder0Carob pulp flour52.5 gCarob share of the listed 300 g ingredient total, calculated here17.5%

Each treatment also contained 75 g margarine, 75 g sugar and 75 g egg; these weights come from the paper's Table 1.[3] **Treatment 30 removed all 15 g of cocoa, added 22.5 g of carob and reduced wheat flour from 60 to 52.5 g.** Treatment 10 removed the cocoa while increasing wheat flour to 67.5 g. This was not a series that changed only the fraction of cocoa replaced.[3]

The final column is a calculation on the listed ingredient total, not the baked product's mass. The materials section mentions baking powder, but Table 1 gives no amount, so the table explains the substitution structure rather than providing a complete replication recipe. Figure 1's caption also labels the control as 15% cocoa on a flour basis, conflicting with Table 1's 15 g ÷ 75 g = 20% and the 20% stated in the text. The comparison here follows the tabulated weights.[3]

Twenty trained panelists assessed the cakes 24 hours after baking, with three samples per person and 12 assessments per treatment. The study used a 15 cm line scale. Overall acceptability averaged 10.4 for treatment 30 and 8.9 for the control, but every treatment shares the letter “a” for this attribute in Table 3. The higher mean does not establish a preference advantage.[3]

Physical properties also need to be read separately. Table 2 gives specific volume as 2.22 ± 0.12 mL/g for the control (a), 1.93 ± 0.00 for treatment 30 (abc) and 1.78 ± 0.10 for treatment 50 (bc). Treatment 30 and the control share a letter and are not significantly different; treatment 50 and the control do not, and treatment 50 has significantly lower specific volume. Failure to detect a significant difference is not evidence of equivalence.[3]

Figure 1 adds an important texture distinction. Treatment 50 had a significantly harder crumb than the control, while treatments 10 and 30 were significantly softer. Treatment 30 did not differ significantly from the control in springiness, **but its cohesiveness was already significantly lower**; this change did not begin only above 30%. Springiness and cohesiveness declined further at treatments 50 and 70.[3]

For a project aiming to retain a relatively soft cake while changing flavor, treatment 30 is a useful trial reference—not an optimum with unchanged texture. The authors also called for a standard acceptance test with 100 consumers to confirm the sensory findings.[3]

A 2018 muffin study used either 5.0% cocoa or 5.0% carob powder. Here, 5% belongs to the authors' listed whole-formula proportions, not a 75 g flour basis. The formula also contained 25.5% soybeans, 6.5% flaxseeds and 6.0% wheat flour.[4] The soybeans were soaked for 12 hours, cooked for 45 minutes and blended. They should not be interpreted as 25.5% dry soy flour; the paper does not clearly state whether that proportion was weighed before or after soaking.[4]

In a nine-point hedonic test with 78 volunteers, carob muffins scored 7.1 and cocoa muffins 6.9, with no statistically significant difference.[4] A separate descriptive assessment by ten trained panelists found the carob muffins sweeter, less bitter and weaker in cocoa taste, with stronger beany and “unknown” taste notes.[4] The development opportunity is a different flavor that remains acceptable, not a promise that substitution will go unnoticed.

The muffin scores should not be compared numerically with the cake scores: a nine-point hedonic scale and a 15 cm line scale were used with different participants and recipes.[3][4] Neither study lowered added sugar as part of its carob comparison. The muffin formula retained 19.0% white sugar, and each cake formula retained 75 g sugar. Greater perceived sweetness is not a successful sugar-reduction trial.[3][4]

Pulp powder is the relevant candidate for changing cocoa flavor. If the task is thickening or stabilizing an aqueous system, investigate seed-endosperm-derived locust bean gum, or LBG, separately. CAROB S.A. differentiates its [PALGUM range](https://carob.es/en/product) by viscosity, particle size and color, and describes synergistic interactions with xanthan and carrageenan.[1]

Request the exact grade and its test conditions. EFSA's 2017 scientific opinion describes LBG as swelling in cold water and requiring heating for maximum solubility; this does not prescribe one hydration temperature and time for every commercial grade.[5] The food-grade section of the public PALGUM page also does not provide a complete viscosity test protocol.[1]

One further distinction matters: Nordmann's [VISCOGUM CGP](https://www.nordmann.global/en/news-events/news/exquisite-carob-products-from-morocco) is a seed-derived protein flour, described commercially as containing 40–50% protein and promoted for emulsification. LBG-VISCOGUM on the same page is locust bean gum. The shared VISCOGUM name does not make them the same ingredient, and the protein range is not a test report for a purchased batch.[2]

Keep the existing formula as a control, then select medium roast, dark roast or a separate Raw candidate according to the desired flavor. In the first comparison, hold other conditions constant and record carob, cocoa and wheat flour in grams. Record both the powder-fraction percentage and the percentage of all weighed ingredients. Compare baked color, sweetness, cocoa taste, specific volume, softness and cohesiveness before deciding whether to change roast or inclusion level.

A useful purchasing conversation can start with: “We want to reduce this cocoa powder while retaining this color and texture.” That gives a supplier more to work with than “30% carob.” Third-party products illustrate selection options; actual supply specifications, documentation and samples still require confirmation.

Product-positioning comparison: eight Amazon.com search records for “carob powder,” including three detail-page samples (27 September 2026). Brand descriptions inform sample selection; no blind tasting or same-formula product comparison was performed.[9]

H&F lists Classic CM 203 as a protective colloid for low-viscosity fermented milk drinks, alongside other grades intended for gels and yoghurt texture.[11] That application distinction matters when a low-sugar drink needs to remain thin.
## Fermented flaxseed: read the detection limit before “complete removal”

A 2026 kimchi study used flaxseed processed with a defined Lactobacillaceae consortium, followed by degumming and drying, before incorporation into kimchi.[2] It therefore does not show that simply adding raw flaxseed to a fermented food will achieve the same result.

Other details limit direct transfer: the work describes a 1 kg flaxseed batch and calls for further industrial-scale validation; its abstract says eight weeks of kimchi fermentation, while methods and results describe six weeks.[2] The addition levels of 0.5%, 1.0% and 2.0% refer to the seasoning mixture, not the weight of the entire kimchi product.[2] These findings support further process investigation, not a ready-made inclusion recommendation.

For an extruded meal intended for a cereal or bakery development project, evaluate residual cyanogenic content alongside the meal's oil, flavour and storage behaviour. For a lignan-rich extract, keep the marker assay and cyanogenic assay separate, and confirm whether the quoted concentration belongs to the starting meal, the dried extract or the supplied blend. For a fermented material, establish the complete process history and the meaning of every “ND” result before comparing it with a heat-treated grade.
[2] Fermented flaxseed in kimchi: analytical limits and process scope

The recommended addition is on the cold side, typically before filtration. For addition before or during filtration, the supplier gives examples of up to 3 mL/hL for bottom-fermented beers and up to 6 mL/hL for top-fermented beers. These refer to the supplied product, not undiluted hop oil: they equal up to 0.03 and 0.06 mL/L respectively. The sheet proposes small additions to bottled beer with a microliter syringe to help establish a suitable amount.[5]

Iso-Extract is an aqueous solution of potassium salts of iso-alpha acids, specified at 30.0 ± 2.0% by mass by HPLC. It is intended for post-fermentation bitterness adjustment. Its sheet warns against prediluting the full-strength concentrate with beer because the lower pH causes precipitation, while recommending dosing into the beer stream where vigorous mixing is assured.[7]

The paper calls the process “fermentation,” while also discussing high-sugar osmotic conditions as inhibiting microbial growth.[2] Its measurements establish a time-dependent composition in this particular fruit–sugar preparation, not a selected-microorganism mechanism or probiotic effect. The liquid-sample values also have a different mass basis from the dry seed and pulp results above.

For the milk exemption, HMRC includes animal milk, reconstituted or recombined milk, fermented milk, buttermilk and specified whey forms; cream is not included in its definition of milk.[4] A formulation record should consequently distinguish actual qualifying milk from cream, creamer and the overall quantity of dairy-derived ingredients. “Contains dairy” is not a substitute for that record.

The 2028 draft also contains a specific drinking-yoghurt exclusion: at least 90ml fermented milk per 100ml prepared drink, with no other liquids added for the purpose of making it more drinkable.[7] Adding yoghurt to a tea drink is not enough to establish that exclusion. Products close to this boundary need the actual formulation and process reviewed against the final text.

选角豆粉，先说清楚想保留哪一种可可风味。Worldwide Botanicals的两款商品就做了不同定位：[中焙](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07JX6YCKR)对应普通可可、牛奶巧克力风味的配方，[深焙](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0F67QBGL3)对应深色可可、黑巧克力风味的配方。这是卖家的选用建议，不是两款粉已经通过了等效替代测试。[6][7]
这一分法比笼统地寻找“可可替代品”更有用。它让第一轮选样有了方向；但要确定加多少、是否调整小麦粉、成品会不会变紧实，还得回到具体配方。两项烘焙研究恰好说明：**接受度相近，不等于味道相同；论文里的百分比，也不一定是可可替换率。**[3][4]
<table class="carob-table">
商品及ASINWorldwide Botanicals中焙，B07JX6YCKR页面如何定位以“regular cocoa”和需要牛奶巧克力风味的配方作为参照。[6]选样时值得验证什么在目标蛋糕中，甜味、可可味及烘烤香气是否协调？
商品及ASINWorldwide Botanicals深焙，B0F67QBGL3页面如何定位以“dark cocoa”和需要黑巧克力风味的配方作为参照。[7]选样时值得验证什么成品是否达到所需深色和风味，而不只是原粉看起来更深？
商品及ASINThe Australian Carob Co.，B01D2975KS页面如何定位标题以“Raw”定位，品牌为The Australian Carob Co.；详情采样不含商品要点。[8]选样时值得验证什么如果项目本来就要开发角豆自身的风味，是否值得与焙烤款并列试样？
中焙和深焙属于同一品牌，适合用来理解卖家怎样按目标风味区分产品；Raw款则不能当作这个品牌的“第三档焙度”。跨品牌比较还会混入原料和加工差异，不能把所有差别都归因于是否焙烤。[6][7][8] Raw款的详情采样中，商品类型为“Video Game”，与标题不相符；因此这里只采用标题及品牌作定位观察，不据此确认加工温度、营养或品质。[8]
更重要的是，“牛奶巧克力风味场景”不等于能按重量直接替掉配方中的牛奶巧克力；“dark cocoa”也没有在这些页面中被定义为某个碱化度或pH规格。[6][7] 因此，选样单应写明原配方用的是可可粉还是巧克力，以及需要保留的风味，而不要只写“用中焙”或“用深焙”。

这三款页面给出了产品定位，却没有构成同配方的性能对照。我们的比较不采用其中的健康、低热量、节省成本或“完美替代”宣称，也不从搜索位置和评论数推算销量。工业原料端同样有焙度选择：[Nordmann介绍的Carob Ingredients果肉粉](https://www.nordmann.global/en/news-events/news/exquisite-carob-products-from-morocco)分浅、中、深焙，列出的应用包括烘焙食品和可可类饮品；其页面没有给出三种焙度的同配方对比结果。[2]
2020年的Madeira型蛋糕研究使用Creta Carob的商业焙烤角豆粉，而不是上面三款零售样品。研究把小麦粉、可可粉和角豆粉合计的75克作为100%粉体基准。[3]
<table class="carob-table">
各组另有75克人造黄油、75克糖和75克蛋，以上克数来自原论文表1。[3] **30组已经完全去掉15克可可粉，加入22.5克角豆粉，并把小麦粉从60克减到52.5克。** 10组则在去掉可可的同时，把小麦粉增加到67.5克；这不是一系列只改变可可替换率的实验。[3]
表中最右列只对列明的配料总量做换算，不是烘焙后成品的质量分数。论文材料部分列有泡打粉，但表1未给出其用量，因此这张表适合解释配比，不能作为完整复刻配方。图1图注把对照的可可用量写成粉体基准的15%，也与表1的15克÷75克＝20%及正文20%不一致；这里采用表1克数。[3]
蛋糕感官试验由20名受训评价员完成，每人评3个样品，每组得到12次评价，测试在烘焙24小时后进行。研究使用15厘米线性量表：30组总体接受度均值10.4，对照8.9，但表3所有组别该指标的显著性字母均为a，不能据此说30组更受欢迎。[3]
物性结果也需要分项读。表2中，对照比容为2.22±0.12 mL/g（a），30组为1.93±0.00（abc），50组为1.78±0.10（bc）。30组和对照共享字母，未显示显著差异；50组和对照不共享字母，比容显著较低。未检出显著差异并不证明两者等效。[3]
图1给出的质构信息更细：50组蛋糕芯比对照显著更硬，10组和30组则显著更软；30组的弹性与对照未显示显著差异，**但内聚性已经显著低于对照**，并非要到超过30%时才发生变化。50组、70组的弹性和内聚性进一步降低。[3]
因此，若目标是在改变风味的同时保留较柔软的蛋糕，30组可以作为配方试验的参考点，而不是“质构不变”的最佳用量。原作者也提出，应再做100名消费者的标准接受度测试来确认感官结果。[3]
2018年的玛芬研究分别使用5.0%可可粉或角豆粉。这里的5%属于作者列出的整个配方比例，不是75克粉体基准；配方还含25.5%大豆、6.5%亚麻籽和6.0%小麦粉。[4] 大豆先浸泡12小时、煮45分钟再打碎，不能把它直接理解成25.5%的干大豆粉；论文没有清楚说明这一比例在浸泡前还是浸泡后称量。[4]
78名志愿者在九分喜好量表上给角豆玛芬7.1分、可可玛芬6.9分，两者无统计显著差异。[4] 另由10名受训评价员进行的描述性评价显示，角豆样品更甜、苦味和可可味较弱，豆味及未明确命名的味道（原文“unknown”）更明显。[4] 这说明开发可以以“不同但仍受欢迎”为目标，而不必承诺消费者尝不出替换。
这项玛芬研究与前面的蛋糕研究也不能互比分数：一个是九分喜好量表，一个是15厘米线性量表，评价人群和配方都不同。[3][4] 两项研究的外加糖都没有随角豆用量降低——玛芬白糖为19.0%，蛋糕各组糖均为75克；甜味变化并不是减糖成功的证据。[3][4]
如果采购目的是改变可可风味，考察的是果肉粉；如果目标是增稠或稳定含水体系，才需要单独考察种子胚乳来源的角豆胶（locust bean gum，LBG）。CAROB S.A.的[PALGUM系列](https://carob.es/en/product)按黏度、粒径和颜色区分等级，厂家还介绍了与黄原胶、卡拉胶复配的协同作用。[1]
询样时应要求完整牌号和测试条件。EFSA的2017年科学意见描述，LBG在冷水中膨胀，达到最大溶解程度需要加热；这并没有规定所有商业牌号统一的水化温度和时间。[5] PALGUM公开页也未在食品级部分给出完整的黏度测试方法及条件。[1]

另外，Nordmann的[VISCOGUM CGP](https://www.nordmann.global/en/news-events/news/exquisite-carob-products-from-morocco)是种子蛋白粉，商业页面标示蛋白含量40–50%并推广乳化用途；同页的LBG-VISCOGUM则是角豆胶。不能仅凭VISCOGUM这个名称把两者当成同一种原料，40–50%也不是所购批次的实测报告。[2]

When replacing leaf-extracted steviol glycosides with enzymatically produced Reb M or a fermentation-derived ingredient, price and “≥95% total glycosides” are not enough. Different EU entries anchor their assays to eleven glycosides together, Reb M alone, Reb D plus Reb A, or a total that includes glucosylated derivatives. The same percentage does not necessarily measure the same substances.[1]

| Fermentation, E 960b(i) | A simple sugar source fermented by *Yarrowia lipolytica* VRM (CBS 147477), followed by purification | At least 95% Reb M, D, A and B together on the dried basis—not at least 95% Reb M alone.[1][4] |

**An enzyme made by fermentation does not make the final glycoside a sugar-fermentation product.** The E 960c definitions above start from leaf-derived glycosides, whereas E 960b(i) starts with fermentation of a simple sugar source. Follow the complete substrate-to-product process, rather than the phrase “fermentation technology”.[1]

The supplementary-specification section of the 2025 issue 11 gazette gives an enzymatic-route organism table using *E. coli* K-12 and refers the other quality specifications for that item to Announcement 2024 No. 2. It separately describes fermentation-derived material, including glucose as substrate, an inactivation step and total steviol glycosides at ≥95.0% on the dried basis.[9] Request the announcement, organism and donor information corresponding to the supplier’s actual process; do not treat organism tables from different announcements as interchangeable attachments for one process.

FSANZ’s **12 May 2021 A1207 approval report** provides a concrete example: Amyris’s fermentation-derived Reb M met the described purity parameters but not the particular production method in the existing specification, prompting an amendment to that specification. The case concerned production method, without extending existing permitted food categories or maximum use levels.[11]

FSANZ’s consumer explanation, updated **26 November 2025**, distinguishes leaf extraction, enzymatic conversion of leaf extracts and fermentation from sugar, while giving labelling examples such as “sweetener (960)”.[10] Consumer ingredient wording therefore need not identify the manufacturing route; procurement still needs the process dossier. Neither document replaces a current Code check for a particular purchased material, and EU E-number suffixes should not be imported as Australian/New Zealand labelling requirements.
